summary: Deep technical discussion focused on Redwood's multi-region routing and failover design for MediCore. Covered policy-based routing, regional capacity accounting, KV cache replication/consistency, batching, quantization tradeoffs in failover scenarios, VPC/on-prem constraints, and concrete DR playbook steps (detection, failover, warm-up, rollback). Agreed on action items: runbook, traffic numbers, canary test, and shared benchmarks.
topics: KV cache replication vs local prefix caching
batching and latency SLOs during failover
transcript:
[00:00] Liam Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We'll do a deep dive on multi-region routing and the failover playbook. Priya and I will cover the runtime implications, caching, and steps for a canary.
[00:22] Anika Rao: thanks Liam. quick context - we run MediCore's inference in us-east-1 primary, eu-west-1 for europe traffic, and we have compliance saying patient data must stay in eu for eu users. we want automatic failover if a region degrades but avoid violating data residency.
[00:45] Priya Singh: got it, and we'll make sure the runbook calls out residency constraints. real quick, wanted to confirm: during normal ops you use with sticky session affinity or based on geolocation?
[00:55] Tom Martinez: geolocation-based mostly, but we do some session affinity for long-running chats. our SLO is p95 < 120ms token latency for interactive flows and batch jobs can be a few seconds.
[01:15] Liam Chen: ok, good. so there are three big buckets: routing policy, regional capacity (and how we account for it), and DR steps including cache warming and model fallbacks. we'll go through each.
[01:30] Priya Singh: first, routing: Redwood supports policy routing - you can express rules like prefer region by latency, fallback by capacity, or pin by customer tier. those policies run in the control plane and are enforced at the gateway. if us-east latency spikes we can route to eu-west for non-eu users, or to a Dedicated pool in another region.
[01:52] Anika Rao: question: what about data residency? if eu user is forced to us-east in failover that breaks compliance.
[01:58] Priya Singh: right - rules can include constraints. for example, rule: if user.region == EU then allow only EU replicas; if EU capacity < threshold then trigger manual escalation to compliance, or fallback to degraded functionality like returning a sanitized response or local on-prem inference. you can also configure allowed-fallbacks per customer.
[02:22] Tom Martinez: sounds reasonable. how do you detect region failure? is it health-check-based or synthetic traffic?
[02:30] Liam Chen: a combination. health heartbeats from the serving pool plus synthetic probes from multiple vantage points. we use circuit-breaker thresholds (error rate, p95 latency, timeouts). when thresholds breach, control plane triggers re-routing decisions. detection windows are configurable - default is 30s to avoid flapping.
[02:50] Priya Singh: also important - graceful degradation. instead of a hard cut, we'll shift percentage based routing: 20% of traffic to fallback first, monitor errors, then ramp. that's our canary pattern.
[03:05] Jared Liu: how about KV cache? We rely heavily on prefix/KV caching for long chats; cross-region failover will invalidate caches and cause huge cold-start token spikes.
[03:18] Priya Singh: yes, that's the tricky part. we recommend region-local caches for low-latency; cross-region synchronous replication adds too much latency and cost. instead we do hybrid: local cache + async replication of hot keys plus heuristics to pre-warm cache on failover.
[03:36] Liam Chen: concrete example: suppose session affinity is pinned to us-east and us-east fails, the control plane re-routes to eu-west. Redwood will, as part of the failover playbook, attempt to fetch session KV from a secure store (encrypted at rest) if allowed by policy; otherwise we fall back to prefix re-generation with a short warmup. the runbook includes steps to progressively increase batch windows to amortize token cost while caches warm.
[03:59] Anika Rao: fetching KV crosses data residency lines for us. can we instead do on-prem cache replication?
[04:07] Priya Singh: we can support Private deployment (VPC/on-prem) for EU - in that case the KV stays local. for hosted multi-region failover you can block cross-region KV access per tenant. the tradeoff is higher cold-start cost during failover.
[04:22] Tom Martinez: when you say warmup, what patterns do you use? naive replay of recent prompts?
[04:27] Priya Singh: warmup strategies include: replay a small set of synthetic prefixes that represent high-frequency patterns, backfill top-K hot keys asynchronously, and use batched prefix reconstruction - we start with larger batching windows (say 2x normal) for the first 60s to reduce per-token overhead.
[04:45] Liam Chen: important runtime note - increasing batch windows lowers cost but raises latency. we recommend dynamic batching thresholds during failover only for lower tiers or non-interactive flows. for interactive SLOs we keep batch windows small and accept higher CPU/GPU utilization for short periods.
[05:02] Jared Liu: quantization - can we use lower precision models as fallback to get more capacity? what's the latency/cost tradeoff?
[05:10] Priya Singh: yes, model variants are a first-class fallback: you can route to a quantized fp16/int8 variant in another region or Dedicated pool. Quantized variants reduce memory and often increase throughput but may slightly change output quality. We measure quality regressions with eval prompt sets and gate rollout if regressed.
[05:31] Tom Martinez: how do you handle model weights and artifacts across regions? sync time can be big for large models.
[05:37] Liam Chen: we keep regional mirrors for common model versions; syncing is done via incremental artifact diffs and pre-stage windows. For new model launches we recommend a pre-warm period where you push artifacts to regional caches during low traffic. for emergency failover, we provide lightweight compatible variants that are smaller and fast to pull.
[05:56] Anika Rao: network egress cost is a big worry if you cross-region for traffic. do you have cost controls?
[06:02] Priya Singh: yes, routing policies can include cost ceilings. you can set hard caps on cross-region egress, or prefer cheaper fallbacks like local quantized models. we also provide per-route cost reporting in Console so you can see egress impact.
[06:18] Tom Martinez: operationally, during a regional outage, what's the recommended DR playbook? stepwise?
[06:25] Liam Chen: we put a recommended playbook in the runbook. high-level steps: 1) detection & assess impact (automated health checks + on-call confirmation), 2) initial traffic steering (gradual 10-20% to fallback), 3) observe SLOs and errors for 3-5 minutes, 4) ramp to 50/100% if stable, 5) if KV cold starts happen, trigger cache warmup jobs and increase batching briefly, 6) if compliance prevents cross-region, trigger manual policy or local on-prem fallback, 7) once primary heals, drain fallback and perform cookie/affinity reconciliation. we include rollback criteria (error rate back above threshold, model-quality regressions).
[07:06] Priya Singh: we add automation: a playbook task that automatically spins up dedicated emergency capacity in a cold-region if configured (subject to quota), and toggles routing. there's also a manual override.
[07:18] Anika Rao: what about consistency of audit logs and observability across regions? we need a central audit trail for compliance; can't have logs split.
[07:27] Liam Chen: logs are replicated to a central, tamper-evident store and are available per-tenant. retention and encryption policies are configurable. for Private deployments we provide an options to forward to your SIEM.
[07:40] Tom Martinez: is there support for draining and connection handoff for long-lived KV sessions?
[07:45] Priya Singh: we do a draining process: when a node is being removed we signal session migration hooks - but full transparent migration of large KV state is expensive. recommended approach: checkpoint session state to secure store periodically so fallback nodes can resume. for strict residency, checkpointing stays in-region.
[08:03] Jared Liu: Do you have recommendations for health-check thresholds? our worry is flapping causing unnecessary failovers.
[08:10] Liam Chen: yes, use multi-signal checks with rolling windows: require 2 of 3 signals (synthetic error rate, p95 latency, instance heartbeat) and a min window of 30s. exponential backoff for re-join helps avoid flaps. Also set a cool-down window after a failover (e.g., 5-10 minutes) before attempting automatic revert.
[08:33] Priya Singh: also test regularly - scheduled chaos exercises. runbook suggests quarterly failover drills and at least one canary per release.
[08:44] Tom Martinez: how does batching behave across regions during failover when capacity is tight?
[08:50] Priya Singh: runtime supports dynamic batching heuristics per pool. During failover we can temporarily increase max batch size and longer micro-batching windows to improve throughput at the cost of tail latency. For interactive paths you can keep smaller batch caps. We surface batch metrics in Console so you can correlate batching window increases with latency changes.
[09:12] Anika Rao: we'd like a concrete example: we have 2000rps baseline, 1-hour outage in us-east, 30% traffic is EU-only, remaining global. what's a recommended policy?
[09:24] Liam Chen: recommended: 1) Pin EU users to eu-west always; 2) for global users, prefer nearest region but set fallback to Dedicated in us-west or quantized eu-west if capacity allows; 3) set cross-region egress cap to a fixed monthly budget so cost doesn't spike; 4) enable automatic gradual ramping (10% -> 50% -> 100% over 3-10 minutes) with health gates; 5) prewarm critical model artifacts in failover nodes before ramp to 50%.
[09:58] Jared Liu: for testing, can Redwood run a simulated outage and replay our last 24h traffic to benchmark failover latency?
[10:04] Priya Singh: yes, we can run a canary replay in a staging setup - we'll need your traffic sample and SLOs. we'll run two tests: cold failover (no cache) and warm failover (prewarmed caches) and produce a benchmark spreadsheet.
[10:18] Liam Chen: next, security: for Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS and HSM; for hosted, we use envelope encryption and can integrate with your KMS via federation. cross-region key access is gated by policy.
[10:32] Tom Martinez: for EU-only customers, can you ensure no metadata leaves region?
[10:36] Priya Singh: yes - set tenant-level residency. metadata and logs stay in-region; cross-region replication is disabled. that's a Private/Dedicated configuration or strict hosted tenancy with region locks.
[10:48] Anika Rao: any gotchas with autoscaling during failover? sudden scale ups create queue spikes, right?
[10:54] Liam Chen: autoscaling is driven by both queue length and observed tail latency; during failover, autoscaling can lag, so we recommend pre-reserving burst capacity (reserved Dedicated cap) or accelerate scaling policies for critical routes. also pre-warm GPU kernels for expected model types to reduce cold launch time.
[11:16] Tom Martinez: how long to spin up extra capacity typically? GPUs can take minutes.
[11:20] Priya Singh: cold GPU provisioning can be several minutes; with warm pools it's 20-40s for most kernels. that's why we recommend options: a) Dedicated reserved burst capacity for DR, b) smaller quantized fallback that fits in cheaper instances, or c) keep a pool of warm nodes in a secondary region.
[11:38] Jared Liu: do you support partial model fallbacks, like routing heavy token flows to cheap models but keeping critical NLU in full model?
[11:45] Liam Chen: yes - route by route/model granularity. you can map routes to model families and specify failover models. e.g., high-value customer route -> no fallback (manual only); low-value route -> quantized fallback.
[11:58] Priya Singh: we'll add a sample policy config in the runbook.
[12:03] Anika Rao: what's the expected user impact during a planned maintenance vs unplanned outage?
[12:09] Priya Singh: planned maintenance: you can drain and pre-warm fallbacks, so user impact should be minimal. unplanned: expect temporary latency spikes and possibly degraded outputs while caches warm and capacity scales. runbook prioritizes critical routes to minimize user-facing impact.
[12:25] Tom Martinez: any recommended SLA wording for multi-region failover?
[12:29] Liam Chen: we typically commit to regional uptime for primary region and provide a separate availability target for multi-region failover paths. we'll share sample SLA language.
[12:37] Anika Rao: ok great. can you share the runbook and the benchmark plan?
[12:41] Liam Chen: yes - action items captured. We'll share: runbook draft, benchmark spreadsheet template, and a recommended policy config. we'll also propose dates for the canary run.
[12:52] Priya Singh: quick note - some transcriptions below use wrong product names occasionally; when we send runbook we'll include the exact API flags and Console screenshots.
[13:01] Tom Martinez: cool. thanks everyone.
[13:05] Liam Chen: recap of next steps: Priya share runbook by 7/18, Tom provide traffic/SLOs by 7/20, Jared provide VPC/topology by 7/21, schedule canary for 7/22. we'll also attach a link to a sample policy and the benchmark template. thanks all.
[13:28] Anika Rao: thanks, bye.
[13:31] (meeting ends)
